title: Doubtful debts
examples: What is the difference between a provision and an actual bad debt?

explain.say: Today we learn about doubtful debts in accounting.

items: Doubtful debts are amounts owed by customers.
Some customers might not pay their bills.
We must estimate this potential loss.

explain.say: First we look at making a provision for doubtful debts.
A provision is an estimated amount of money lost.
Next we deal with actual bad debts that occur.

items: Step 3: Write off as Bad Debt

explain.say: If a debt is confirmed uncollectible it is written off.

draw.text: Write-off: Removing bad debt from books

explain.say: In real life a shopkeeper might estimate losses.

items: Sales Credit | Estimated Loss | Provision Made

faq.q: What is the difference between making a provision and writing off a bad debt?
faq.a: A provision is an estimate recorded before the loss happens. Writing off is the actual removal of a debt after it is confirmed lost.
asks: When do I record a provision?
How is a provision different from a write-off?

faq.q: Do I record the bad debt expense directly to the profit and loss account?
faq.a: No, first you create the provision, and then you account for the actual bad debt against that provision.
asks: Where does the bad debt expense go?
Should I debit or credit the provision account?

faq.q: Is it always necessary to make a provision for doubtful debts?
faq.a: It is standard accounting practice to estimate potential losses to give a true view of assets.
asks: What if I don't estimate anything?

faq.q: Can I estimate the provision based on the total sales?
faq.a: Yes, often a percentage of total credit sales is used as the basis for the provision.
asks: Is sales percentage okay for estimation?

faq.q: What happens to the provision when the debt is finally collected?
faq.a: If the debt is collected after being written off, you reverse the write-off entry, which increases your revenue.
asks: What if the money comes back?
How do I reverse a write-off?

facts: A provision is an accounting estimate of potential losses.
Bad debts are amounts owed that are deemed uncollectible.
The provision account acts as a contra-asset account.
The provision is estimated based on historical data or experience.

quiz.say: A company estimates it might lose five percent of its total receivables. If receivables are one hundred thousand dollars, what is the provision?
quiz.why: You multiply the total receivables by the estimated percentage loss.

wrong.0: This is only 0.5 percent, which is too low an estimate.
wrong.1: This is the total amount, not the estimated loss.
wrong.2: You must account for the risk of non-payment.

quiz.say: A debt of two thousand dollars is confirmed lost. Which account is debited?
quiz.show: Write-off: Debit the bad debt account

options.show: Bad Debts Expense (or Bad Debts Account)
options.say: Bad Debts Expense (or Bad Debts Account)

quiz.why: The expense account records the actual loss incurred by the business.

wrong.0: Cash is only involved when the debt is actually collected.
wrong.2: You debit the receivable only if you are correcting an error.
wrong.3: The provision is credited when you write off the debt.

quiz.say: If a business writes off a debt and later collects it, what is the accounting treatment?

options.show: Debit Cash and Credit Accounts Receivable
options.say: Debit Cash and Credit Accounts Receivable

options.show: Debit Bad Debts Expense and Credit Cash
options.say: Debit Bad Debts Expense and Credit Cash

options.show: Debit the Provision account, then Credit the receivable
options.say: Debit the Provision account, then Credit the receivable

quiz.why: You reverse the initial write-off by crediting the provision account.

wrong.0: This ignores the previous write-off entry made in the books.
wrong.1: This records the income as a new expense, which is incorrect.
wrong.2: You must record the recovery to show the true income.
